extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent attorneys (computer-implemented and biotechnology inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether claimed subject-matter qualifies as statutory invention under section 2 of the Patent Act across computer-related (GUIs, data structures, databases, CAD, signals) and biotechnology domains. Explains how claim form, claim elements, and technological contribution affect patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of claim determines statutory subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office distinguishes between claims by their form (e.g., data structure per se, computer program per se, physical memory storing software, method/process, device/manufacture) when determining whether subject-matter is within the definition of 'invention' in section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that is in form a data structure or computer program per se is generally non-statutory (disembodied). A claim directed to a physical memory storing software or to a device operating the method is in form a statutory manufacture or device, but may still fail if the inventive contribution is non-statutory. Examine whether claimed non-statutory elements limit the technological nature of a statutory element; perform a contribution analysis comparing discrete elements to the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical user interface (GUI) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A GUI per se is directed to excluded subject-matter by its form; even if generated by a computer program, the claim may still be objected to under section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A method claim that includes statutory steps (e.g., displaying graphical elements and dynamically retrieving information) which together provide a technological solution (e.g., dynamic querying to keep control options current) can be statutory. If the method steps operate together to provide a unitary technological result and are novel/inventive over the prior art, the method may be patentable. If the method is patentable, corresponding device or memory claims that implement the method may also be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data structures per se are non-statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office considers a data structure to be an abstract idea or plan for organizing data items and not to include the physical medium upon which it is stored; a data structure per se is disembodied and not an invention within section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a data structure to affect patentability it must in some way limit the technological nature of a statutory element in the claim. A claim defining a data structure alone is directed to non-statutory subject matter by its form. A computer-implemented method using the data structure that changes the technological character of a step (e.g., prioritizing packets using the structure) may be statutory if novel and inventive. A physical memory storing data does not alter the technological character of the memory unless the stored data is part of executable code that renders the computer more efficient or reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical memory storing data versus executable code
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim to a physical memory is a statutory manufacture in form, but the nature of the stored content matters: data stored on the memory does not alter the technological character of the memory, whereas executable computer code that makes the computer more efficient may do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the inventive contribution is merely the data, the memory claim may include a discrete non-statutory element and be objected to under section 2 after contribution analysis. If the memory stores executable code that imparts a technological effect (e.g., improves efficiency, reliability), that software-on-physical-memory element can be a statutory contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Databases and database management systems (DBMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A database is interpreted as solely a collection of information and a database per se is disembodied and not an invention within section 2. A database management system is generally understood to be a computer program and thus a computer program per se is not statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim to a physical memory storing a DBMS defines a statutory manufacture in form, but the inventive contribution must alter the technological character of a statutory element. A claim to a system or server that includes software means that provide new technological functionality (e.g., load-tracking control server distributing requests according to server load and synchronizing during light load) can be statutory if the software is novel and inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-clauses interpreted as software on physical memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of 'means for ...' are understood to be software stored on a physical memory and executed by a processor when describing server/software features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'means' both alter the technological operation of the server (if the software provides new functionality) and can be treated as statutory 'software on a physical memory' elements. Alternatively, the means-modified server may be considered a single discrete statutory element. Patentability then hinges on whether that server/software element is novel and inventive over the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution analysis for mixed statutory/non-statutory claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim includes both statutory elements (machines, memories, methods) and non-statutory elements (data structures, databases, signals, programs per se), the examiner should perform a contribution analysis to determine whether the claim as a whole contains a statutory contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-statutory features are treated as discrete elements of the claim. If the inventive aspect is non-statutory, object under section 2 of the Patent Act. If the combination of elements (including statutory elements modified by software) provides a technological solution that is novel and inventive, the claim may be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-aided design (CAD) programs and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: CAD programs are specialized computer programs used as tools by designers and may comprise a technological contribution; methods of designing may be viewed as schemes or mental processes which are disembodied and not a practical invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventions related to CAD usually focus on the CAD program functionality as a tool. If the CAD method provides a technological solution to a practical problem (e.g., hierarchical optimisation that reduces operations and avoids false minima), the computer-implemented method can be statutory. A CAD program per se (computer program claim) is defective in form unless tied to a statutory medium or device that embodies a technological contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for implementation detail to show technological contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed steps are essentially known calculations or procedures, merely performing them on a computer does not necessarily provide a statutory contribution; explicit details of how the computer performs the operations or how a technological obstacle is overcome may be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sequence of operations to perform the calculations would have been self-evident to a person skilled in the art, there is no technological innovation in enabling the computer to perform them and an objection under section 2 is appropriate. Where implementation details show the computer performs operations in a novel way that overcomes a technical obstacle, these should be claimed to support patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals (electromagnetic and acoustic) are non-statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office regards electromagnetic and acoustic signals and waveforms to be forms of energy and not material products; claims to signals per se do not constitute statutory subject-matter within section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals are transitory in nature. Once information in a signal has been stored on a physical medium it is more appropriately referred to as data; however, claims defining a physical medium storing a signal or waveform are considered indefinite under section 27(4). Methods, processes, machines or manufactures involved in generation, transmission, reception, or processing of signals may be patentable if other patentability criteria (novelty, inventiveness, technological contribution) are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Device/transceiver claims that include software-enabled encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: A device claim (e.g., a transceiver) that recites means for encoding, transmitting and decoding where some means relate to hardware and others to software may be statutory if the software-enabled encoding modifies technological character and provides a technical advantage (e.g., high-rate transmission while minimizing interference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the software-enabled encoding is novel and inventive, the overall device claim can be allowable because the claim does not include a discrete non-statutory element; evaluate novelty and inventive step of all defined elements in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher vs lower life forms (biotechnology subject-matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: For section 2 purposes, life forms are divided into lower life forms (statutory) and higher life forms (non-statutory), generally based on whether they are unicellular (lower) or multicellular (higher). Animals at any stage of development are considered non-statutory higher life forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower life forms (e.g., microscopic algae, unicellular fungi, bacteria, protozoa, viruses, transformed cell lines, hybridomas, embryonic/multipotent/pluripotent stem cells) are generally statutory as manufactures or compositions of matter. Higher life forms (animals, plants, mushrooms, fertilized eggs, totipotent stem cells) are non-statutory. A claim should expressly exclude higher life forms where necessary (e.g., where a cell claim could be construed to include a fertilized egg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims including higher life forms may be salvageable by purposive construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim not directed to a higher life form per se but including a higher life form within its scope (e.g., as a component of a composition, as a use) may, depending on purposive construction, be statutory subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, a claim to 'an animal feed comprising X' construed as the use of X is likely statutory even if X is a higher life form. When construed as X or a product comprising X, the claim will be non-statutory if X is a higher life form. Where X has been processed by significant chemical or physical modification, the claim may be construed as a manufacture and be statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stem cells and developmental potential nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: A stem cell which is embryonic, multipotent or pluripotent is not alone capable of developing into an animal and is considered to be a lower life form; fertilized eggs and totipotent stem cells are included in the higher life form proscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim to a cell could reasonably be understood as encompassing a fertilized egg or totipotent stem cell, that subject-matter should be expressly excluded by proviso, otherwise the claim may be construed as including matter excluded from section 2. Claims construed as isolated cells do not need to specify 'as found in the laboratory' or 'in isolated form.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Organs and tissues generally non-statutory
rubrics_metrics.description: Organs and tissues (whether of plant or animal origin) are generally not considered to be manufactures or compositions of matter for purposes of section 2 of the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organs and tissues are typically created by complex processes with elements requiring no human intervention and do not consist of ingredients combined or mixed together. Claims directed to organs or tissues should be treated accordingly under subject-matter analysis.
